newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to give dialogue a chance.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to give dialogue a chance.

text.p: Serbia's drawn-out political crisis appeared on Thursday to be nearing an end after opposition leaders promised they would stop their street protests once parliament had restored their municipal election victories.
"We will stop the protests and will give a chance to dialogue if parliament approves the bill," Vuk Draskovic told reporters in Paris after meeting French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

Meanwhile, about 15,000 students paraded through a foggy Belgrade for the 79th day, keeping up pressure on President Slobodan Milosevic to deliver on his promise to recognise the results of November's municipal elections in Belgrade and 13 other Serbian towns.
In a sudden announcement on Tuesday, Serbia's authoritarian leader wrote to his prime minister asking parliament to reinstate the disputed results.
On Wednesday, the government approved the draft law to be put to parliament next Tuesday in what most political analysts believed would be a mere formality.
But Draskovic, invited to Paris for talks with de Charette along with the two other opposition leaders, has taken a cautious line, wary of any attempt at subterfuge by the Socialist authorities.
"We must be very, very careful. We had very bad experiences of Mr Milosevic in the past," Draskovic said, speaking in English.

He said that all three Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders had agreed to a dialogue with Milosevic on their other outstanding demands, including freeing Serbian media from state control and establishing the independence of the country's courts.
Both parliamentary and presidential elections are due to be held by the end of this year and, while municipalities have very limited powers, they control regional electronic media.

De Charette, echoing the views of other Western leaders, said Serbia's problems should be resolved by recognition of the election results, dialogue between government and opposition, free access to the media and democratic elections.

Milosevic's ruling Socialists had annulled the November election results on grounds of "irregularities", prompting massive street protests by the opposition, students and other professional groups and drawing sharp international criticism.

Diplomats and analysts warned that next Tuesday was still far off and that hardliners, who apparently suffered a major set-back with Milosevic's decision, could try and wreck the move by forcing or provoking a crackdown on the protesters.

On Sunday, paramilitary police swooped upon unsuspecting and peaceful protesters. Repeated baton charges, backed up by water cannon, left scores injured and the Serbian government's international credibility in tatters.
Senior political sources say that Milosevic had already made the decision to reinstate Zajedno's victory last weekend.

They say Milosevic did not order Sunday's police action but met top police chiefs on Monday, ostensibly to praise their handling of a different matter but in fact "to sort out the mess". His letter to the prime minister was published the next day.
Foreign governments have given a cautious welcome to Milosevic's decision to reinstate the disputed results.

Former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who led a fact-finding mission to Serbia on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation (OSCE) in Europe to study the election issue, was guarded in his response.
"We can only congratulate ourselves if they (the report's recommendations) are fulfilled," he told Spanish radio.

The OSCE chairman, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, said on Wednesday: "The decision (to recognise the opposition election gains) is hopefully a step towards positive democratic development in... Yugoslavia. The installation of the elected candidates is expected without delay."
Draskovic said Milosevic's decision was "Good. What is not good is the fact that Mr Milosevic did this after 80 days of peaceful demonstrations all over Serbia".
He added that if Milosevic failed to carry through democratic reforms "it would be very easy for us to have 100,000 people on the streets of Serbia overnight."

The three opposition coalition leaders -- Draskovic, Vesna Pesic and Zoran Djindjic -- were expected to address a rally of their supporters in central Belgrade on Thursday night on their return from Paris.
